title: The Quiet Grocery Conquest: Inside Patel Brothers' Push Into America's Fastest-Growing Suburbs
excerpt: From a single Chicago storefront in 1974 to over 50 locations nationwide, the largest Indian grocery chain in America is following the diaspora into suburbs that never had a dal section — and reshaping what neighbourhood grocery stores look like.
body:
When Swetal Patel describes the new 20,000-square-foot Patel Brothers store taking shape in St. Johns County, Florida, he sounds less like a grocery executive and more like a diaspora ambassador. "This has been something the community has been wanting and asking for," he told *WhatNow* in January. "We're looking forward to expanding our footprint in the Florida market."

The St. Johns store — which will anchor a retail centre at the Shops at Racetrack Road, complete with a Patel's Fresh Kitchen bakery, a sit-down restaurant, a jewellery store, and a beauty shop — is not an isolated play. It is part of a systematic expansion by America's largest Indian grocery chain into exactly the kind of fast-growing suburbs where the Indian-American population has quietly boomed over the past decade.

## From Chicago to Everywhere

Founded in 1974 by brothers Mafat and Tulsi Patel, the chain began as a modest storefront on Devon Avenue in Chicago — a strip that remains one of the densest concentrations of South Asian commerce in the Western Hemisphere. Half a century later, Patel Brothers operates more than 50 stores across the United States and three in Canada, with a third generation of the Patel family now steering day-to-day operations.

The company's recent moves suggest a strategy that tracks directly with U.S. Census patterns. In Florida, the St. Johns County store — a 4.25-acre, purpose-built anchor — will supplement the existing Jacksonville location on Baymeadows Road. Swetal Patel has confirmed that at least three additional Florida locations are in the pipeline, though specifics remain under wraps.

In Texas, where the Indian-American population has grown by more than 60 per cent in the past decade, Patel Brothers is preparing its first Austin location, expected in the second half of 2026. And in Ohio, India Grocers — a separate chain that shares the same demographic tailwinds — is converting a former Big Lots property on Dublin's Sawmill Road corridor into a full-service South Asian marketplace.

## More Than Groceries

What sets these new-generation Indian grocers apart from the cramped, fluorescent-lit shops that older NRIs remember is ambition. The St. Johns location will include an in-house bakery turning out fresh naan, samosas, and Indian-style pizzas daily. Patel's Fresh Kitchen counters, now a standard feature of new builds, serve ready-to-eat biryani, curries, and sweets — a concession to younger diaspora consumers who want the flavours of home without the three-hour Sunday cooking marathon.

"This will be a very modern-looking store, with the new design we've launched in the last four to five years," Swetal Patel said of the St. Johns project. That design language — clean lines, wider aisles, bilingual signage — signals a chain that is courting not just the aunties who have always known where to find asafoetida, but the broader American consumer newly obsessed with global flavours.

## The Numbers Behind the Naan

The timing is not accidental. Indian cuisine is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to food-industry data firm Dataessential, and the U.S. ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion. Patel Brothers is positioning itself at the intersection of two powerful currents: a diaspora that has grown large enough to sustain speciality retail in second- and third-tier metros, and a mainstream curiosity that has moved Indian food from "exotic" to "essential."

The chain's expansion also reflects a broader pattern in American retail. As legacy discount retailers like Big Lots retreat from suburban strip malls, international grocers are snapping up the vacated square footage — a dynamic visible in India Grocers' Dublin move and in the proliferation of H Mart and 99 Ranch stores in similar corridors.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the NRI family in St. Johns County or suburban Austin, a Patel Brothers opening is more than a convenience. It is a signal that their community has arrived — that the critical mass of desi families in the area has crossed the threshold where the market comes to them, rather than the other way around.

"At Patel Brothers, our mission is to bring the best ingredients from South Asia, right to your doorstep," the company's website reads. Increasingly, that doorstep is in a suburb that, a generation ago, had never seen a fresh curry leaf.

## What's Next

With three undisclosed Florida locations in the works and Austin on the horizon, Patel Brothers appears to be accelerating. The question is no longer whether Indian grocery stores can thrive outside traditional diaspora hubs like Edison, New Jersey, or Artesia, California. It is whether they can become neighbourhood anchors in the same way that H Mart has for Korean communities — a cultural institution disguised as a grocery run.
